BLADE: Scalable Bi-level Adaptive Data Selection for LLM Training

Jiaxing Wang ††thanks: Equal Contribution. Email: wangjiaxing41@jd.com    Jin Xu Affiliation:  University of Oxford Email: xiangdeping1@jd.com    Zirui Liu Affiliation: Deping Xiang Affiliation:  Affiliation: JD.com Email: liuzirui.17@jd.com    Zicheng Zhang Affiliation: Deping Xiang Affiliation:  Affiliation: JD.com Email: zhangzicheng6@jd.com    Guoqiang Gong,  Jun Fang,   Chao Liu,   Pengzhang Liu  ,   Tongxuan Liu ††thanks: Corresponding to Pengzhang Liu Affiliation: Deping Xiang Affiliation:  Affiliation: JD.com Email: gongguoqiang1@jd.com    Ke Zhang Affiliation: Deping Xiang Affiliation:  Affiliation: JD.com Email: liupengzhang@jd.com    Qixiang Jiang Affiliation: Deping Xiang Affiliation:  Affiliation: JD.com Email: liutongxuan1@jd.com Affiliation: Renmin University of China Affiliation: University of Chinese Academy of Sciences Email: zhangke323@jd.com Email: jiangqixia@jd.com Email: jin.xu@stats.ox.ac.uk
Abstract

As Large Language Model (LLM) datasets scale to trillions of tokens, data selection has emerged as a critical frontier to filter out uninformative noise and construct adaptive learning trajectories. Beyond static heuristic filtering, advanced data selection methods for LLM training largely follow two paradigms, each with fundamental limitations. Influence-based methods provide principled bi-level objectives but require intractable inverse-Hessian computations, while excess-loss methods are computationally efficient but rely on a static reference model that becomes misaligned with the evolving proxy model during training. We propose BLADE (Bi-Level Adaptive Data sElection), a Hessian-free framework for data selection. BLADE reformulates the bi-level optimization problem underlying influence-based methods as a penalized single-level objective via Lagrange multipliers, avoiding inverse-Hessian computation while revealing a principled connection to excess-loss based data selection. The resulting objective recovers an excess-loss form but replaces the static reference model with a dynamic one that stays synchronized with training. Theoretically, we prove that this penalized formulation guarantees first-order convergence. For efficient online batch selection, we instantiate BLADE as a memoryless randomized block-coordinate Frank-Wolfe algorithm. Extensive experiments show that BLADE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art data selection baselines, providing a practical recipe for LLM training.

   

1 Introduction

The remarkable capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) are fundamentally driven by the scale and quality of their pre-training data. However, as available corpora reach trillion-token scales, naively training on the entirety of these datasets often yields diminishing returns, as low-quality, noisy, or highly redundant tokens can degrade model reasoning capabilities Zhou et al. (2023); Engstrom et al. (2024). This makes data selection, the problem of choosing informative, high-signal training examples that best improve performance, a central problem in LLM training.

Existing model-aware data selection methods for LLM training largely follow two paradigms. Influence-based methods estimate how each training example affects validation loss, yielding a principled bi-level formulation of data selection Xia et al. (2024); Yu et al. (2024b). However, they require approximating inverse-Hessian terms arising from the bi-level objective, making them computationally prohibitive at LLM scale. Excess-loss methods avoid this cost by scoring examples through the loss gap between a proxy model and a reference model Mindermann et al. (2022); Lin et al. (2024). Yet the reference model is typically trained a priori and kept fixed, causing stale selection signals as the proxy model evolves. More broadly, the relationship between these paradigms remains unclear: influence-based methods are theoretically grounded but difficult to scale, while excess-loss methods are efficient but lack a principled connection to the bi-level data selection objective.

We introduce BLADE (Bi-Level Adaptive Data sElection), a framework that bridges the principled bi-level formulation of influence-based methods with the scalability of excess-loss-based approaches. Starting from the bi-level objective, BLADE avoids differentiating through the full inner training problem by incorporating the inner optimality condition into the outer objective via Lagrange multipliers. The resulting penalized formulation eliminates the need for inverse-Hessian approximation and reveals a principled connection to excess-loss formulation: data are scored by the discrepancy between a proxy model trained on selected training data and a reference model that also incorporates validation information. Unlike conventional excess-loss methods, BLADE does not use a reference model trained a priori and kept fixed. Instead, it dynamically synchronizes the reference model with the evolving proxy model throughout training. This allows BLADE to retain the bi-level foundation of influence-based methods while matching the scalability and online efficiency of excess-loss-based data selection.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We introduce BLADE, a Hessian-free reformulation of bi-level data selection that converts the bi-level objective into a penalized single-level problem via Lagrange multipliers, eliminating the need for inverse-Hessian approximation. BLADE enjoys first-order convergence guarantees.

  • •

    We show that BLADE bridges the two dominant paradigms for LLM data selection by deriving an excess-loss-style selection criterion from the bi-level objective and replacing the fixed reference model used in prior excess-loss methods with a dynamic reference model synchronized with the evolving proxy model.

  • •

    For efficient online batch selection, we instantiate BLADE as a memoryless randomized block-coordinate Frank-Wolfe method. Extensive experiments across various LLM training scenarios show that it consistently accelerates convergence and outperforms existing data selection baselines.

2 Methodology

In this section, we present BLADE, a Hessian-free framework for bi-level adaptive data selection. We start from a rigorous bi-level formulation of data selection and derive a penalized single-level objective, which we subsequently instantiate as an efficient online token-level selection algorithm. Figure 1 illustrates the overall procedure, and the complete workflow is provided in Algorithm 1. The notations used in this paper are summarized in Appendix E.

2.1 Problem Formulation

Consider training an LLM on a dataset 𝒟t​r​a​i​n={xn}n=1N\mathcal{D}_{train}=\{x_{n}\}_{n=1}^{N}. In the context of dense autoregressive LLM training, we define the selection unit nn at the token level. Thus data selection refers to the problem of finding the optimal subset of informative tokens. We encode this decision using a continuous relaxation of the selection vector, defining the feasible set as 𝒜:={𝜶∈[0,1]N|∑n=1N𝜶n=γ​N}\mathcal{A}:=\left\{\boldsymbol{\alpha}\in[0,1]^{N}|\sum_{n=1}^{N}\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{n}=\gamma N\right\} 11 1 While data selection is inherently discrete, this continuous relaxation mathematically establishes a differentiable, gradient-based bi-level optimization objective. Crucially, as we will show in Section 2.2, our choice of optimization algorithm naturally projects these continuous variables back onto discrete extreme points (𝜶∈{0,1}N\boldsymbol{\alpha}\in\{0,1\}^{N}), seamlessly bridging continuous theory with discrete data selection., where γ\gamma is the keeping ratio. For any selection vector 𝜶\boldsymbol{\alpha}, let w⁡(𝜶)w(\boldsymbol{\alpha}) denote the optimal model parameters obtained by minimizing the weighted training loss. Our goal is to minimize the validation loss ℒval​(w​(𝜶))\mathcal{L}_{\text{val}}(w(\boldsymbol{\alpha})) over 𝜶\boldsymbol{\alpha}, yielding the following bi-level optimization problem:

min𝜶∈𝒜⁡ℒval​(𝒘⁡(𝜶)):=ℒval​(𝒘⁡(𝜶)) s.t. 𝒘​(𝜶)∈arg⁡min𝒘​ℒtrain​(𝜶,𝒘):=1γ​N​∑n=1N𝜶n​ℒtrainn​(𝒘).\min_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}\in\mathcal{A}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{val}}(\text{\boldmath{$w$}}(\boldsymbol{\alpha})):=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{val}}\left(\text{\boldmath{$w$}}(\boldsymbol{\alpha})\right)\ \ \text{ s.t. }\text{\boldmath{$w$}}(\boldsymbol{\alpha})\in\arg\min_{\boldsymbol{w}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{train}}(\boldsymbol{\alpha},\text{\boldmath{$w$}}):=\frac{1}{\gamma N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{n}\mathcal{L}_{\text{train}}^{n}(\boldsymbol{w}). (1)

Intuitively, the outer-level problem seeks the optimal token composition to minimize validation loss, constrained by model weights optimized on the inner-level reweighted training loss.

2.2 BLADE: Hessian-Free Bilevel Data Selection

Solving the bi-level optimization problem (1) is challenging due to its nested structure. By viewing the inner-level problem as a constraint and subsequently incorporating it into the outer-level problem as a Lagrangian penalty, Equation (1) can be reformulated as a single-level problem Shen and Chen (2023); Kwon et al. (2023); Wang et al. (2025):

min𝜶∈𝒜,𝒘⁡ℋλ​(𝜶,𝒘):=ℒval​(𝒘)+λ⁡(ℒtrain​(𝜶,𝒘)−min𝒖⁡ℒtrain​(𝜶,𝒖)).\min_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}\in\mathcal{A},\boldsymbol{w}}\mathcal{H}_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{\alpha},\boldsymbol{w}):=\mathcal{L}_{\text{val}}(\boldsymbol{w})+\lambda\left(\mathcal{L}_{\text{train}}(\boldsymbol{\alpha},\boldsymbol{w})-\min_{\boldsymbol{u}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{train}}(\boldsymbol{\alpha},\boldsymbol{u})\right). (2)

Here, the auxiliary variable 𝒖\boldsymbol{u} is introduced as a proxy of 𝒘⁡(𝜶)∈arg⁡min𝒘​ℒtrain​(𝜶,𝒘)\boldsymbol{w}(\boldsymbol{\alpha})\in\arg\min_{\text{\boldmath{$w$}}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{train}}(\boldsymbol{\alpha},\text{\boldmath{$w$}}). The constraint in Equation (1) is transferred into the penalization ℒtrain​(𝜶,𝒘)−min𝒖⁡ℒtrain​(𝜶,𝒖)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{train}}(\boldsymbol{\alpha},\text{\boldmath{$w$}})-\min_{\boldsymbol{u}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{train}}(\boldsymbol{\alpha},\boldsymbol{u}). As justified by Proposition 3 in (Shen and Chen, 2023), by properly invoking the penalty parameter λ→∞\lambda\to\infty, the solution of Equation (2) rigorously approximates the original bi-level problem in Equation (1) (see Appendix A for details).

Algorithm Procedure

Optimizing Equation (2) involves coordinating three variables: the data selection indicator 𝜶\boldsymbol{\alpha}, a proxy model 𝒖\boldsymbol{u}, and a reference model 𝒘w.

Update on 𝒖\boldsymbol{u} (Proxy Model): Given current batch of data, determined by 𝜶(t)\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{(t)}, we approximate the 𝒖∈arg⁡min𝒖​ℒtrain​(𝜶(t),𝒖)\boldsymbol{u}\in\arg\min_{\boldsymbol{u}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{train}}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{(t)},\boldsymbol{u}) in the penalization term with one gradient step:

𝒖(t+1)=𝒖(t)−ηu​∇𝒖ℒtrain​(𝜶(t),𝒖(t))\boldsymbol{u}^{(t+1)}=\boldsymbol{u}^{(t)}-\eta_{u}\nabla_{{\boldsymbol{u}}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{train}}\left(\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{(t)},\boldsymbol{u}^{(t)}\right) (3)

(green line with arrow in Figure 1). The proxy model is trained on the selected training data and maintained through the whole data selection process.

Update on 𝒘\boldsymbol{w} (Reference Model): The reference model 𝒘w serves to capture signals from both the training and validation distributions. Based on the 𝒘w-dependent terms in Equation (2), the update rule becomes:

𝒘k+1(e)=𝒘k(e)−η𝒘​(∇𝒘ℒval​(𝒘k(e))+λ​∇𝒘ℒtrain​(𝜶(e​τ),𝒘k(e))),\boldsymbol{w}^{(e)}_{k+1}=\boldsymbol{w}^{(e)}_{k}-\eta_{\boldsymbol{w}}\left(\nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{val}}\left(\boldsymbol{w}^{(e)}_{k}\right)+\lambda\nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{train}}\left(\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{(e\tau)},\boldsymbol{w}^{(e)}_{k}\right)\right), (4)

To avoid an overly erratic reference model, 𝒘w is updated periodically every τ\tau steps of training 𝒖\boldsymbol{u}. We introduce an episode index e=⌊t/τ⌋e=\lfloor t/\tau\rfloor to denote the current update cycle. To control the optimization disparity between 𝒘w and 𝒖\boldsymbol{u}, we synchronize their starting points by setting 𝒘0(e)=𝒖(e​τ)\text{\boldmath{$w$}}_{0}^{(e)}=\boldsymbol{u}^{(e\tau)} at the beginning of each episode. After running Equation (4) for KK steps (orange line in Figure 1), the finalized reference model 𝒘~(e)=𝒘K(e)\tilde{\text{\boldmath{$w$}}}^{(e)}=\text{\boldmath{$w$}}_{K}^{(e)} is utilized for data selection during the subsequent τ\tau steps.

Update on 𝜶\boldsymbol{\alpha} (Data Weights): The term related to 𝜶\boldsymbol{\alpha} is λ⁡(ℒtrain​(𝜶,𝒘)−min𝒖⁡ℒtrain​(𝜶,𝒖))\lambda\left(\mathcal{L}_{\text{train}}(\boldsymbol{\alpha},\boldsymbol{w})-\min_{\boldsymbol{u}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{train}}(\boldsymbol{\alpha},\boldsymbol{u})\right). That says, the 𝜶\boldsymbol{\alpha} update seeks a solution to Equation (2) by finding data that aligns the training loss with the validation-informed reference model. Recall that ℒtrain​(𝜶,⋅)\mathcal{L}_{\text{train}}(\boldsymbol{\alpha},\cdot), by definition, is the 𝜶\boldsymbol{\alpha} weighted token-wise loss, taking the gradient w.r.t 𝜶\boldsymbol{\alpha} and applying Frank Wolfe update yields:

𝜶(t+1)=𝜶(t)+η𝜶(𝒔(t)−𝜶(t))where𝒔=argmin𝜶∈𝒜⟨ℒtrain1:N(𝒘~(e))⏟reference model−ℒtrain1:N(𝒖(t))⏟proxy model,𝜶⟩\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{(t+1)}=\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{(t)}+\eta_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}(\boldsymbol{s}^{(t)}-\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{(t)})\ \text{where}\ \boldsymbol{s}=\arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}\in\mathcal{A}}\left\langle\underbrace{\mathcal{L}_{\text{train}}^{1:N}\left(\tilde{\boldsymbol{w}}^{(e)}\right)}_{\textbf{reference model}}-\underbrace{\mathcal{L}_{\text{train}}^{1:N}\left(\boldsymbol{u}^{(t)}\right)}_{\textbf{proxy model}},\boldsymbol{\alpha}\right\rangle (5)

Let Δ∈ℝN\Delta\in\mathbb{R}^{N} denote the hyper-gradient vector w.r.t 𝜶\boldsymbol{\alpha}, where its nn-th element is the token-level loss difference Δn=ℒtrainn​(𝒘)−ℒtrainn​(𝒖)\Delta_{n}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{train}}^{n}(\text{\boldmath{$w$}})-\mathcal{L}_{\text{train}}^{n}(\boldsymbol{u}) 22 2 For simplicity, here we omit the subscription of the reference model 𝒘w and proxy model 𝒖\boldsymbol{u}.. A larger loss gap indicates that the token is highly informative for aligning the proxy model with the validation data, thus prioritizing it for selection.

Convergence Analysis

Because the objective is non-convex and constrained over 𝜶∈𝒜\boldsymbol{\alpha}\in\mathcal{A}, we evaluate its first-order stationary convergence using the Frank-Wolfe Gap, which serves as the standard convergence measure for conditional gradient methods in non-convex settings Lacoste-Julien (2016); Reddi et al. (2016). The theoretical convergence of our method is summarized below.

Theorem 1 (Informally).

Under standard regularity assumptions (PL condition, smoothness, bounded Hessians, detailed in Appendix A), 𝛂(t)\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{(t)} obtained in the BLADE algorithm converges to a first-order stationary point of the bi-level objective (1) in the rate of 𝒪⁡(T−14)\mathcal{O}(T^{-\frac{1}{4}}) by properly selecting λ,K,η𝛂,η𝐰\lambda,K,\eta_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}},\eta_{\text{\boldmath{$w$}}}, and η𝐮\eta_{\boldsymbol{u}}.

The proof is left in Appendix A. Theorem 1 indicates that BLADE theoretically ensures the optimality of the selected data.

The Frank-Wolfe algorithm provides an intrinsic property to bridge our continuous optimization with the discrete reality of data selection: the Linear Minimization Oracle (LMO, solving for 𝒔\boldsymbol{s} in Equation (5)) naturally projects the update onto the extreme points of the constraint set 𝒜\mathcal{A}. Taking a greedy step size (ηα=1\eta_{\alpha}=1) yields a perfectly sparse, binary closed-form solution:

𝜶n(t+1)=ITop-​γ​N​(−Δn(t))\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{n}^{(t+1)}=I_{\text{Top-}\gamma N}(-\Delta_{n}^{(t)}) (6)

meaning 𝜶n(t+1)=1\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{n}^{(t+1)}=1 if the loss gap −Δn(t)-\Delta_{n}^{(t)} ranks in the Top-γ​N\gamma N, and 00 otherwise, perfectly recovers our data selection scenario.

BLADE Admits Online Batch Selection

While Equation (6) establishes the optimal data selection over the global dataset of size NN, evaluating the full hyper-gradient Δ\Delta across billions of tokens is computationally cumbersome. To transition to a scalable practical implementation, we efficiently optimize 𝜶\boldsymbol{\alpha} by instantiating BLADE as a memoryless Randomized Block-Coordinate Frank-Wolfe method Lacoste-Julien et al. (2013); Reddi et al. (2016); Hazan and Kale (2012). At each iteration, we uniformly sample a candidate batch ℬc​a​n​d(t)\mathcal{B}_{cand}^{(t)}, that is, effectively selecting a block of coordinates from the high-dimensional vector 𝜶\boldsymbol{\alpha}. Applying the Top-KK (K=γ​|ℬc​a​n​d(t)|K=\gamma|\mathcal{B}_{cand}^{(t)}|) greedy selection strictly within this sampled subset serves as a stochastic, online approximation of the global bi-level objective. Beyond mere computational efficiency, this online batch curation Mindermann et al. (2022); Lin et al. (2024); Wang et al. (2024) aligns perfectly with the non-stationary dynamics of LLM training. It acts as an adaptive curriculum, allowing the data selection to continuously synchronize with the evolving capabilities of the proxy model. Finally, to preserve the structural integrity and autoregressive dependencies of the attention context window during LLM training, tokens with 𝜶n=0\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{n}=0 are not physically discarded from the sequence. Instead, the binary decision acts as a token-level loss mask (as in RHO-1 Lin et al. (2024)). This masking mechanism ensures that BLADE can orchestrate a fine-grained, dynamic token curriculum without disrupting the sequential causality of the language model.

2.3 BLADE Unifies and Improves Existing Data Selection Methods

Our BLADE framework elegantly bridges the gap between the two dominant paradigms in data selection: the theoretical rigor of influence-based methods Pan et al. (2024); Yu et al. (2024b) and the computational efficiency of excess-loss-based methods Mindermann et al. (2022); Lin et al. (2024). By inspecting their core selection criteria, we demonstrate how BLADE unifies these approaches while systematically addressing their respective limitations.

Unifying Influence-Based Paradigms:

Influence-based methods prioritize data by estimating a sample’s impact on validation loss. Mathematically, by invoking Cauchy’s Implicit Function Theorem, evaluating the influence function is equivalent to computing a snapshot of the hyper-gradient of our exact bi-level objective (Equation (1)) from a uniform initial state (𝜶n=1N\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{n}=\frac{1}{N}):

∂ℒval∂𝜶n∝−∇𝒘ℒtrainn​(𝒘)T​𝑯−1​∇𝒘ℒval​(𝒘)\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}_{\text{val}}}{\partial\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{n}}\propto-\nabla_{\text{\boldmath{$w$}}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{train}}^{n}(\text{\boldmath{$w$}})^{T}\text{\boldmath{$H$}}^{-1}\nabla_{\text{\boldmath{$w$}}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{val}}(\text{\boldmath{$w$}})

where 𝑯H is the Hessian of the training objective (ℒtrain\mathcal{L}_{\text{train}}) (see Appendix B for the full derivation). In this sense, existing influence-based methods are essentially attempting to approximate the solution to our bi-level formulation. However, exactly computing this inverse-Hessian product at scale is intractable, forcing prior work to rely on brittle approximation techniques Pan et al. (2024); Xia et al. (2024) or auxiliary influence predictors Yu et al. (2024b). Instead, BLADE formally addresses the root bi-level optimization problem by reformulating it into a penalized single-level objective (Equation (2)). This entirely bypasses the inverse-Hessian computation, providing a framework that retains the principled foundation of influence-based methods while achieving superior computational efficiency.

Improving Excess-Loss Paradigms:

Excess-loss methods select training samples by computing the loss gap between a proxy model and a reference model trained solely on validation data. As outlined in Table 1, BLADE recovers this highly tractable scoring mechanism but fundamentally improves the reference architecture. Standard excess-loss approaches (like RHO-1) rely on a static reference model trained a priori, which inherently stagnates and loses its discriminative power as the proxy model evolves during training. In contrast, BLADE introduces a dynamic reference model that periodically synchronizes with the proxy model. This dynamism ensures the reference remains competitive and accurately calibrated throughout the learning trajectory, mitigating the risk of lagging.

3 Related Work

Data selection is attracting increasing attention as a pivotal strategy for developing LLMs with comprehensive and balanced capabilities. Our work builds upon two primary strands of research: data selection paradigms and bi-level optimization.

Data Selection

Early approaches to data selection primarily relied on static heuristics Raffel et al. (2020); Rae et al. (2021), diversity sampling Tirumala et al. (2023), and distribution matching Xie et al. (2023) to filter out noisy or out-of-domain data. These methods, nevertheless, fail to align with the target tasks or the model’s specific training dynamics. To achieve model-aware selection, recent advancements have predominantly bifurcated into influence-based and excess-loss-based paradigms. Influence-based methods leverage the influence function Koh and Liang (2017) to quantify a sample’s exact impact on validation loss. While theoretically principled, computing the inverse Hessian-vector products is intractable at the LLM scale. Consequently, methods like LESS Xia et al. (2024) and G-DIG Pan et al. (2024) resort to gradient matching or layer-wise approximations, while MATES Yu et al. (2024b) trains a lightweight surrogate data influence predictor. Alternatively, excess-loss-based methods Mindermann et al. (2022) (and their token-level extension, RHO-1 Lin et al. (2024)) avoid this computational bottleneck by scoring data based on the loss gap between a proxy model and a well-trained reference model. Yet, their reliance on an a priori trained, static reference model inherently upper-bounds the target model’s capability as it evolves.

Comparison of the computational complexity of these strategies is given in Table 2 33 3 We assume backward takes 2×\times computation as the forward process., where CC is the complexity of one step training of a model. TT is the update number of 𝜶\boldsymbol{\alpha}. We explicitly unpack the dominant overhead of MATES as Tprobe×Tvalτ\frac{T_{\text{probe}}\times T_{\text{val}}}{\tau}, which represents the multiplicative cost of oracle data influence collection. Specifically, TprobeT_{\text{probe}} denotes the number of probing samples, and TvalT_{\text{val}} is the number of steps to evaluate each sample’s influence on the entire validation set. This nested complexity arises because MATES requires a full pass over the validation data to label its surrogate model for every probing sample, making it inapplicable for token-level selection. Typically, for relatively large validation data, the overall computational cost of these methods is of the order: MATES > BLADE ≈\approx RHO-1.

Bi-level Optimization

Bi-level optimization provides a rigorous mathematical framework in many scientific disciplines, yet solving it remains challenging due to the nested dependencies between the upper and lower-level problems. Standard gradient-based bi-level solvers Mathieu et al. (2022); Choe et al. (2024); Shaban et al. (2019); Grazzi et al. (2023); Chen et al. (2021); Hong et al. (2023) require estimating implicit gradients, introducing Hessian-vector products (HVPs) that are computationally prohibitive for large-scale neural networks. To mitigate this, recent works like BLISS Hao et al. (2025) employ very small proxy models for HVP estimation, while PBCS Zhou et al. (2022) utilizes policy gradients to bypass HVPs entirely, though it requires training the inner problem to convergence at every outer step. More recently, penalized methods Shen and Chen (2023); Kwon et al. (2023); Kwon et al. (2024) have pioneered reformulating the inner-level problem into a regularized penalty, enabling pure first-order gradient-based optimization. While theoretically elegant, their practical application and scalability within massive LLM pre-training pipelines have remained largely unexplored. BLADE bridges this gap, adapting the penalized bi-level formulation into a highly scalable, Hessian-free framework specifically tailored for token selection.

4 Experiments

In this section, we compare BLADE to state-of-the-art algorithms in Section 4.2. Then we analyse the effectiveness of each design ingredient in Section 4.3. Code will be released upon acceptance.

4.1 Experimental Setup

We consider two distinct continual pre-training scenarios: domain specialization (domain-shift) and general capability enhancement. Complete hyper-parameter settings are provided in Appendix C.

Domain-Shift pre-training:

To evaluate BLADE’s ability to drive domain specialization, we follow Lin et al. (2024) and utilize a blend of MetaMath Yu et al. (2024a) and Mammoth Yue et al. (2024) 44 4 This is a subset of the validation data used in RHO-1 Lin et al. (2024), the other data used as validation in RHO-1 are not open-sourced. as the validation set. The candidate training pool is a 5B randomly sampled subset of OpenWebMath Paster et al. (2024) (∼\sim14B math-related web tokens). We deliberately employ foundational base models TinyLlama-1.1B Zhang et al. (2024) and LLaMA-2-7B Touvron et al. (2023) rather than the heavily optimized SOTA models to ensure that pre-existing, saturated capabilities do not mask the intrinsic efficacy of data selection. Following Lin et al. (2024), selection is executed at the token level with a keeping ratio of γ=0.6\gamma=0.6. The reference model 𝒘w is synchronized periodically (τ=1000\tau=1000). Evaluations are conducted across various math benchmarks: GSM8K Cobbe et al. (2021), MATH Hendrycks et al. (2021), SVAMP Patel et al. (2021), ASDIV Miao et al. (2020), MAWPS Kedziorski et al. (2016), TabMWP (TAB) Lu et al. (2023), MathQA (MQA) Amini et al. (2019), MMLU-STEM Hendrycks et al. (2020) and SAT Azerbayev et al. (2023). This evaluation encompasses diverse question types like multiple-choice and open-ended questions. Experiments are conducted on eight NVIDIA Hopper H-100s.

General pre-training:

To verify that BLADE does not overfit to narrow domains and genuinely improves broad capabilities, we utilize OpenHermes-2.5 Teknium (2023) as the validation set. The candidate training pool is a 5B blend of OpenWebMath Paster et al. (2024) and SlimPajama Soboleva et al. (2023). We evaluate the final trained proxy model on benchmarks prioritizing diversity of capabilities and formats, including MMLU Hendrycks et al. (2020), Hellaswag Zellers et al. (2019), OpenBookQA Mihaylov et al. (2018), WinoGrande Sakaguchi et al. (2020), ARC-Easy and ARC-Challenge Clark et al. (2018), BoolQ abd Kenton Lee et al. (2019) and PIQA Bisk et al. (2020). Following Lin et al. (2024), the evaluation is conducted using lm-evaluation-harness Gao et al. (2024).

4.2 Comparisons with State of the Arts

We benchmark BLADE against robust baselines: Base (the un-trained original model), Base-CT (naive continual pre-training on the full candidate set), Random (training on randomly sampled data), MATES Yu et al. (2024b) (a state-of-the-art influence-based method with an influence predictor), and RHO-1 Lin et al. (2024) (the leading token-level excess-loss-based method). For the baselines, we use the published MATES implementation 55 5 MATES: https://github.com/cxcscmu/MATES. and re-implemented RHO-1.

Domain-Shift Pre-training

During the evaluation, the models are prompted with few-shot chain of thought (CoT) as in Lin et al. (2024). In Table 3 (Upper), we see that BLADE significantly outperforms baselines. For instance, it achieves 29.7 averaged accuracy on TinyLlama-1.1B, surpassing the most competitive RHO-1 by 4.0 and the Base-CT baseline by 13.0. We inspect the scalability of BLADE with a larger llama2-7B model. BLADE consistently outperforms the baselines on 7 out 9 benchmarks, and is comparable on MMLU-STEM. SAT is a very small benchmark, containing only 32 questions, so the accuracy on SAT has high variation.

For wall-clock time, BLADE (494.3 min) takes longer than naive continual training (314.6 min), a necessary trade-off to break the performance ceiling. Yet, among model-aware methods, BLADE is highly efficient: it adds merely 62.8 minutes over the static RHO-1 and is significantly faster than MATES. To prevent doubling peak VRAM, BLADE employs an offloading mechanism, periodically loading the reference model 𝒘w to pre-compute scores for τ\tau steps before unloading it, strictly maintaining the peak VRAM of standard single-model training.

General Pre-training

The evaluation results for the general continuous pre-training scenario are summarized in Table 4. BLADE consistently outperforms competing data selection baselines in 7 out of 8 diverse downstream tasks. Notably, it achieves average accuracy of 51.73%\%, establishing a clear margin of +1.15 over the state-of-the-art RHO-1 method. Despite a small fluctuation on the OBQA task, the substantial gains across tasks validate BLADE’s efficacy.

4.3 Analysis

To evaluate the effectiveness of each design component, we conduct ablation experiments. The model used is the TinyLlama-1B Zhang et al. (2024) unless specified and we test on the domain-shift pre-training scenario. Due to limited space, we focus on the effect of the dynamic reference model, the effect of reference model update interval τ\tau and the keeping ratio γ\gamma, and the synchronization mechanism of 𝒘w and 𝒖\boldsymbol{u}. We also discuss the reusability of the learned data orchestration on models of larger sizes in Appendix D.

The Effect of the dynamic reference model

To empirically validate the dynamic reference mechanism, we trace the selected tokens using a 70B oracle loss (Figure 2) and monitor the evolution of their token-level excess loss (Δ\Delta) distributions (Figure 3). Initially (0–1K steps), both RHO-1 and BLADE exhibit high oracle loss as they aggressively select domain-rich web data to bridge the domain gap. The critical divergence occurs at Step 1000, coinciding with BLADE’s first reference model update. As the proxy model quickly masters foundational domain basics, RHO-1’s static reference lags. Figure 3 illustrates RHO-1’s Δ\Delta distribution collapsing toward zero and negative values, losing its discriminative power and causing its oracle loss to stagnate. Conversely, BLADE recalibrates the reference against the proxy’s growing capabilities, restoring a pronounced right-tail distribution (Δ>0\Delta>0). Guided by this calibrated signal, BLADE continuously targets tokens with genuine positive marginal utility, seamlessly shifting its curriculum from raw vocabulary acquisition to isolating clean, highly structured reasoning tokens, as confirmed by the descent in its oracle loss.

The Effect of τ\tau and γ\gamma:

We systematically evaluate the impact of the reference update interval (τ∈{500,1000,1500,2000}\tau\in\{500,1000,1500,2000\}). As shown in Figure 2, downstream performance remains highly consistent across all tested values. This insensitivity carries significant practical implications: practitioners can safely adopt a larger τ\tau (e.g., 2000) to reduce the computational overhead of maintaining the dynamic reference without sacrificing selection quality. For the keeping ratio, we evaluate BLADE across (γ∈{0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8}\gamma\in\{0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8\}). As illustrated in Figure 2, the model’s average accuracy first increases as γ\gamma goes up to 0.6. Nevertheless, increasing the budget to γ=0.8\gamma=0.8 degrades performance, validating our core premise: an overly high keeping ratio inevitably forces the inclusion of uninformative or redundant noise, degrading the model’s capabilities.

The Effect of Synchronizing 𝒖\boldsymbol{u} and 𝒘w

One obvious characteristic of BLADE is the periodic synchronization of the proxy model 𝒖\boldsymbol{u} and the reference model 𝒘w (w0(e)=u(e​τ)w_{0}^{(e)}=u^{(e\tau)}). We investigate this by tracking the parameter distance Dist​(𝒖,𝒘)=‖𝒖−𝒘‖2\text{Dist}(\boldsymbol{u},\text{\boldmath{$w$}})=||\boldsymbol{u}-\text{\boldmath{$w$}}||_{2} during training. As shown in Figure 4(a), synchronization bounds the disparity between 𝒖\boldsymbol{u} and 𝒘w throughout the selection process. In contrast, maintaining them independently (as in RHO-1) incurs blown-up divergence (Figure 4(b)). Crucially, this bounded drift effectively restricts the optimization space, allowing our framework to enforce the bi-level constraint using a moderate, numerically stable penalty parameter in practice, thereby circumventing the gradient explosion typically associated with λ→∞\lambda\to\infty in continuous theory.

5 Conclusion

In this paper, we propose BLADE, a principled, efficient, and versatile data selection framework for large language model training. Starting from a bi-level formulation, BLADE reformulates the intractable bi-level objective into a penalized single-level surrogate via Lagrange multipliers, thereby eliminating the need for inverse-Hessian computation while retaining the theoretical grounding of influence-based methods. This reformulation also reveals a clear connection to excess-loss-based selection, but crucially replaces the static reference model with a dynamic validation-informed reference model that remains synchronized with the evolving proxy model, avoiding the calibration lag that limits prior approaches. Theoretically, BLADE converges to a first-order stationary point of the bi-level objective at a rate of 𝒪(T−1/4)\mathcal{O}(T^{-1/4}). We further instantiated BLADE as an efficient online selection algorithm through a memoryless randomized block-coordinate Frank-Wolfe procedure, enabling practical token-level selection at LLM scale. Extensive experiments and analysis are conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. Overall, BLADE provides a principled and computationally viable path for dynamic data selection in large-scale LLM training.

Appendix A Convergence of Bi-level Data Selection

Here we present a theoretical analysis of the proposed BLADE. The original bi-level optimization problem

𝒫:min𝜶∈𝒜ℒval(𝒘∗(𝜶)) s.t. 𝒘∗(𝜶)∈S∗(𝜶):=argmin𝒘ℒtrain(𝜶,𝒘)\mathcal{P}:\quad\min_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}\in\mathcal{A}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{val}}\left(\text{\boldmath{$w$}}^{*}(\boldsymbol{\alpha})\right)\ \ \text{ s.t. }\text{\boldmath{$w$}}^{*}(\boldsymbol{\alpha})\in S^{*}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}):=\arg\min_{\boldsymbol{w}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{train}}(\boldsymbol{\alpha},\text{\boldmath{$w$}}) (7)

is difficult to solve due to the imposed hard constraint. We turn to the Lagrangian problem of 𝒫\mathcal{P} such that

𝒫λ:min𝜶∈𝒜,𝒘ℒval(𝒘)+λ(ℒtrain(𝜶,𝒘)−min𝒖ℒtrain(𝜶,𝒖))\mathcal{P}_{\lambda}:\quad\min_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}\in\mathcal{A},\text{\boldmath{$w$}}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{val}}\left(\text{\boldmath{$w$}}\right)+\lambda\left(\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{train}}(\boldsymbol{\alpha},\text{\boldmath{$w$}})-\min_{\boldsymbol{u}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{train}}(\boldsymbol{\alpha},\boldsymbol{u})\right) (8)

There has been a vast body of existing literature [38, 19] discussing the relationship between the Lagrangian problem 𝒫λ\mathcal{P}_{\lambda} and the original problem 𝒫\mathcal{P}.

Specifically, by employing a sufficiently large penalty λ\lambda, the solution to 𝒫λ\mathcal{P}_{\lambda} closely approximates the exact solution to 𝒫\mathcal{P}. Consequently, we can solve the original problem 𝒫\mathcal{P} by optimizing the surrogate 𝒫λ\mathcal{P}_{\lambda}, as we did in this paper.

A.1 The Proposed Algorithm

A full workflow of Bi-Level Adaptive Data sElection (BLADE) is detailed in Algorithm 1. BLADE reformulates the complex data selection problem into a penalized single-level optimization process. Operating directly on incoming streams of candidate data, the algorithm maintains two structurally synchronized models: a proxy model 𝒖\boldsymbol{u} (serving as the target LLM) and a reference model 𝒘w. To evaluate data efficacy dynamically, BLADE computes the loss gap between the reference and proxy models. As the proxy model 𝒖\boldsymbol{u} is trained on 𝒟train\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}} while the reference model 𝒘w is trained on both the train and validation data, the gap between 𝒖\boldsymbol{u} and 𝒘w quantifies the expected gain of incorporating a token towards the target distribution. The tokens with the Top-γ\gamma loss gap are selected subsequently. Notably, the proxy model 𝒖\boldsymbol{u} and reference model 𝒘w are synchronized at the beginning of the periodic update of 𝒘w in BLADE.

A.2 Convergence Rate

Next, we establish the convergence rate of the proposed Algorithm 1. We first establish the following definitions to simplify the notations. We denote

ℋλ​(𝜶,𝒘)=ℒval​(𝒘)+λ⁡(ℒtrain​(𝜶,𝒘)−min𝒘⁡ℒtrain​(𝜶,𝒘)),\mathcal{H}_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{\alpha},\text{\boldmath{$w$}})=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{val}}(\text{\boldmath{$w$}})+\lambda\left(\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{train}}(\boldsymbol{\alpha},\text{\boldmath{$w$}})-\min_{\text{\boldmath{$w$}}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{train}}(\boldsymbol{\alpha},\text{\boldmath{$w$}})\right),

with Sλ∗​(𝜶)={𝒘:𝒘∈arg⁡min𝒘​ℋλ​(𝜶,𝒘)}S_{\lambda}^{*}(\boldsymbol{\alpha})=\{\text{\boldmath{$w$}}:\text{\boldmath{$w$}}\in\arg\min_{\text{\boldmath{$w$}}}\mathcal{H}_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{\alpha},\text{\boldmath{$w$}})\}, and S∗​(𝜶)={𝒘:𝒘∈arg⁡min𝒘​ℒtrain​(𝜶,𝒘)}S^{*}(\boldsymbol{\alpha})=\{\text{\boldmath{$w$}}:\text{\boldmath{$w$}}\in\arg\min_{\text{\boldmath{$w$}}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{train}}(\boldsymbol{\alpha},\text{\boldmath{$w$}})\}. We further define

ℋ⁡(𝜶)=inf𝒘∈S∗​(𝜶)ℒval​(𝒘),\mathcal{H}(\boldsymbol{\alpha})=\inf_{\text{\boldmath{$w$}}\in S^{*}(\boldsymbol{\alpha})}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{val}}(\text{\boldmath{$w$}}), (9)

The minimum of ℋ⁡(𝜶)\mathcal{H}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}) is exactly the solution to original problem 𝒫\mathcal{P} (7). We then impose the following standard regularity conditions to derive the convergence rate:

Assumption 1 (PL condition).

For any 𝛂∈𝒜\boldsymbol{\alpha}\in\mathcal{A}, both ℒtrain​(𝛂,𝐰)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{train}}(\boldsymbol{\alpha},\text{\boldmath{$w$}}) and ℋλ​(𝛂,𝐰)\mathcal{H}_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{\alpha},\text{\boldmath{$w$}}) satisfy the Polyak-Łojasiewicz (PL) inequality with coefficient μ\mu and μλ\mu_{\lambda}, respectively. That says:

ℒtrain​(𝜶,𝒘)−min𝒘⁡ℒtrain​(𝜶,𝒘)≤12​μ​‖∇𝒘ℒtrain​(𝜶,𝒘)‖2\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{train}}(\boldsymbol{\alpha},\text{\boldmath{$w$}})-\min_{\text{\boldmath{$w$}}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{train}}(\boldsymbol{\alpha},\text{\boldmath{$w$}})\leq\frac{1}{2\mu}\left\|\nabla_{\text{\boldmath{$w$}}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{train}}(\boldsymbol{\alpha},\text{\boldmath{$w$}})\right\|^{2} (10)

and

ℋλ​(𝜶,𝒘)−min𝒘⁡ℋλ​(𝜶,𝒘)≤12​μλ​‖∇ℋλ​(𝜶,𝒘)‖2.\mathcal{H}_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{\alpha},\text{\boldmath{$w$}})-\min_{\text{\boldmath{$w$}}}\mathcal{H}_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{\alpha},\text{\boldmath{$w$}})\leq\frac{1}{2\mu_{\lambda}}\|\nabla\mathcal{H}_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{\alpha},\text{\boldmath{$w$}})\|^{2}. (11)

Moreover, the coefficient μλ\mu_{\lambda} satisfies limλ→∞μλλ=1\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\frac{\mu_{\lambda}}{\lambda}=1.

Assumption 2 (Smoothness).

For any 𝛂∈𝒜\boldsymbol{\alpha}\in\mathcal{A},

  1. 1.

    Both ∇𝒘ℒtrain​(𝜶,𝒘)\nabla_{\text{\boldmath{$w$}}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{train}}(\boldsymbol{\alpha},\text{\boldmath{$w$}}) and ∇𝒘ℒval​(𝒘)\nabla_{\text{\boldmath{$w$}}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{val}}(\text{\boldmath{$w$}}) are Lipschitz continuous to 𝐰w on coefficient LL.

  2. 2.

    Both ℒtrain​(𝜶,𝒘)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{train}}(\boldsymbol{\alpha},\text{\boldmath{$w$}}) and ℒval​(𝒘)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{val}}(\text{\boldmath{$w$}}) are Lipschitz continuous to 𝐰w with coefficient BB.

Assumption 3 (Bounded Hessian).

For any 𝛂∈𝒜\boldsymbol{\alpha}\in\mathcal{A}, 𝐰∈S∗​(𝛂)\text{\boldmath{$w$}}\in S^{*}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}), there exists positive constants κ,ρ\kappa,\rho, satisfying Hessian matrices ∇𝐰𝐰2​ℒtrain​(𝛂,𝐰)⪰κ\nabla^{2}_{\text{\boldmath{$w$}}\text{\boldmath{$w$}}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{train}}(\boldsymbol{\alpha},\text{\boldmath{$w$}})\succeq\kappa66 6 For two matrices 𝐀\boldsymbol{A}, 𝐀⪰κ\boldsymbol{A}\succeq\kappa means 𝐀−κ​𝐈\boldsymbol{A}-\kappa\boldsymbol{I} is a positively semi-definite matrix. and ∇𝛂​𝐰2​ℒtrain​(𝛂,𝐰)⪯ρ\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}\text{\boldmath{$w$}}}^{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{train}}(\boldsymbol{\alpha},\text{\boldmath{$w$}})\preceq\rho.

Assumption 4 (Lipschitz Hessian).

For any 𝛂∈𝒜\boldsymbol{\alpha}\in\mathcal{A}, ℒtrain​(𝛂,𝐰)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{train}}(\boldsymbol{\alpha},\text{\boldmath{$w$}}) is twice continuous differentiable, and the Hessian matrices ∇𝛂​𝐰2​ℒtrain​(𝛂,𝐰)\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}\text{\boldmath{$w$}}}^{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{train}}(\boldsymbol{\alpha},\text{\boldmath{$w$}}), ∇𝐰𝐰2​ℒtrain​(𝛂,𝐰)\nabla_{\text{\boldmath{$w$}}\text{\boldmath{$w$}}}^{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{train}}(\boldsymbol{\alpha},\text{\boldmath{$w$}}) are all Lipschitz continuous to 𝐰w with coefficient HH.

The non-negative loss function ℒtrain​(𝛂,𝐰)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{train}}(\boldsymbol{\alpha},\text{\boldmath{$w$}}), ℒval​(𝐰)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{val}}(\text{\boldmath{$w$}}) are uniformly bounded by positive constant DD.

Next, we present a lemma to characterize the gap between the gradient of ∇𝜶ℋ​(𝜶)\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\mathcal{H}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}) and ∇𝜶ℋλ​(𝜶,𝒘)\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\mathcal{H}_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{\alpha},\text{\boldmath{$w$}}).

Lemma 1 (Equality of the bilevel-optimization and the regularized problem [45]).

Under Assumptions 1-4, for any given 𝛂\boldsymbol{\alpha} and 𝐰λ∗​(𝛂)∈Sλ∗​(𝛂)\text{\boldmath{$w$}}_{\lambda}^{*}(\boldsymbol{\alpha})\in S_{\lambda}^{*}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}), it holds

‖∇𝜶ℋ​(𝜶)−∂∂𝜶​ℋλ​(𝜶,𝒘λ∗​(𝜶))‖≤1λ​(H​B2μ2​(ρκ+1)+ρ​L​Bμ​κ)\left\|\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\mathcal{H}(\boldsymbol{\alpha})-\frac{\partial}{\partial{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}}\mathcal{H}_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{\alpha},\text{\boldmath{$w$}}_{\lambda}^{*}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}))\right\|\leq\frac{1}{\lambda}\left(\frac{HB^{2}}{\mu^{2}}\left(\frac{\rho}{\kappa}+1\right)+\frac{\rho LB}{\mu\kappa}\right) (12)

From Lemma 1, we know that the gap between the gradients of original problem ℋ⁡(𝜶)\mathcal{H}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}) and its Lagrange version ℋλ​(𝜶,𝒘λ∗​(𝜶))\mathcal{H}_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{\alpha},\text{\boldmath{$w$}}_{\lambda}^{*}(\boldsymbol{\alpha})) can be extremely small by invoking penalty parameter λ→∞\lambda\to\infty. This implies that we can directly utilize the gradient of the Lagrangian surrogate to perform gradient-based optimization. Next, we illustrate the Lipschitz continuity of 𝒘λ∗​(𝜶)\text{\boldmath{$w$}}_{\lambda}^{*}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}) and 𝒘∗​(𝜶)\text{\boldmath{$w$}}^{*}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}) to 𝜶\boldsymbol{\alpha}.

‖𝒘∗​(𝜶1)−𝒘∗​(𝜶2)‖≤Lμ​‖𝜶1−𝜶2‖,\|\text{\boldmath{$w$}}^{*}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{1})-\text{\boldmath{$w$}}^{*}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{2})\|\leq\frac{L}{\mu}\|\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{1}-\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{2}\|, (13)

for any 𝐰λ∗​(𝛂1)∈Sλ∗​(𝛂1)\text{\boldmath{$w$}}^{*}_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{1})\in S_{\lambda}^{*}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{1}) and 𝐰λ∗​(𝛂2)=arg⁡min𝐰∈Sλ∗​(𝛂1)​‖𝐰−𝐰λ∗​(𝛂1)‖\text{\boldmath{$w$}}_{\lambda}^{*}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{2})=\arg\min_{\text{\boldmath{$w$}}\in S_{\lambda}^{*}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{1})}\|\text{\boldmath{$w$}}-\text{\boldmath{$w$}}^{*}_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{1})\|.

Following the Frank-Wolfe update in BLADE, we utilize the Frank-Wolfe gap to characterize the stationary condition.

Definition 1 (Frank-Wolfe Gap).

The first-order stationarity measure for constrained non-convex optimization is the Frank-Wolfe Gap:

G⁡(𝜶(t))=max𝒔∈𝒜⁡⟨∇𝜶ℋ​(𝜶),𝜶(t)−𝒔⟩G(\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{(t)})=\max_{\boldsymbol{s}\in\mathcal{A}}\langle\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\mathcal{H}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}),\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{(t)}-\boldsymbol{s}\rangle (16)

G⁡(𝜶(t))≥0G(\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{(t)})\geq 0 always holds, and G⁡(𝛂(t))=0G(\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{(t)})=0 if and only if 𝛂(t)\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{(t)} is a first-order stationary point.

Similarly, we denote the Frank-Wolfe Gap for the penalized optimization problem as Gλ​(𝜶(t))=max𝒔∈𝒜⁡⟨∇𝜶ℋλ​(𝜶,𝒘λ∗​(𝜶)),𝜶(t)−𝒔⟩G_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{(t)})=\max_{\boldsymbol{s}\in\mathcal{A}}\langle\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\mathcal{H}_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{\alpha},\text{\boldmath{$w$}}_{\lambda}^{*}(\boldsymbol{\alpha})),\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{(t)}-\boldsymbol{s}\rangle.

The delayed reference model 𝒘~(e)\tilde{\text{\boldmath{$w$}}}^{(e)} is optimized for KK steps at t=e​τt=e\tau and keep fixed for τ\tau steps. The error is the sum of the optimization residual and target drift over τ\tau steps:

≤2​D​(1+λ)μλ​(1−μλLλ)K/2+λ​Lμλ​τ​ηα​D𝒜\displaystyle\leq\sqrt{\frac{2D(1+\lambda)}{\mu_{\lambda}}}(1-\frac{\mu_{\lambda}}{L_{\lambda}})^{K/2}+\frac{\lambda L}{\mu_{\lambda}}\tau\eta_{\alpha}D_{\mathcal{A}}
=𝒪⁡(τ​η𝜶)\displaystyle=\mathcal{O}(\tau\eta_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}})

For the inner proxy model 𝒖\boldsymbol{u}, one step of SGD yields a strict geometric contraction of the residual under the PL condition. Subsequently, the outer data weight α\alpha updates, causing the optimal target to drift. By utilizing the smoothness of ℒtrain\mathcal{L}_{\text{train}} and applying AM-GM to absorb the linear drift into the residual, the inner tracking dynamics can be strictly bounded as:

We then define the global Lyapunov potential function as the weighted sum of the outer penalized objective and the inner optimization residual:

V(t):=ℋλ​(𝜶(t),𝒘λ∗​(𝜶(t)))+c⋅ℛ⁡(𝜶(t),𝒖(t))\displaystyle V^{(t)}:=\mathcal{H}_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{(t)},\text{\boldmath{$w$}}_{\lambda}^{*}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{(t)}))+c\cdot\mathcal{R}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{(t)},\boldsymbol{u}^{(t)})

To compute the difference V(t+1)−V(t)V^{(t+1)}-V^{(t)}, we add Equation (19) and c×c\times Equation (23):

V(t+1)−V(t)\displaystyle V^{(t+1)}-V^{(t)} ≤−η𝜶​Gλ​(𝜶(t))+(c​η𝒖​μ2−c​η𝒖​μ)​ℛ​(𝜶(t),𝒖(t))+𝒪⁡(λ2​η𝜶2)\displaystyle\leq-\eta_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}G_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{(t)})+\left(\frac{c\eta_{\boldsymbol{u}}\mu}{2}-c\eta_{\boldsymbol{u}}\mu\right)\mathcal{R}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{(t)},\boldsymbol{u}^{(t)})+\mathcal{O}(\lambda^{2}\eta_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{2})
=−η𝜶​Gλ​(𝜶(t))−c​η𝒖​μ2​ℛ​(𝜶(t),𝒖(t))+𝒪⁡(λ2​η𝜶2)\displaystyle=-\eta_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}G_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{(t)})-\frac{c\eta_{\boldsymbol{u}}\mu}{2}\mathcal{R}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{(t)},\boldsymbol{u}^{(t)})+\mathcal{O}(\lambda^{2}\eta_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{2}) (24)

Crucially, the coefficient for ℛ⁡(𝜶(t),𝒖(t))\mathcal{R}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{(t)},\boldsymbol{u}^{(t)}) is −c​η𝒖​μ2≤0-\frac{c\eta_{\boldsymbol{u}}\mu}{2}\leq 0. This indicates that under the two-timescale framework, the descent energy provided by the inner SGD perfectly cancels out the gradient errors injected into the outer optimization via AM-GM. Dropping the non-positive term, we obtain a clean global descent bound:

V(t+1)≤V(t)−η𝜶​Gλ​(𝜶(t))+𝒪⁡(λ2​η𝜶2)\displaystyle V^{(t+1)}\leq V^{(t)}-\eta_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}G_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{(t)})+\mathcal{O}(\lambda^{2}\eta_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}^{2})

≤D𝒜⋅∥∇𝜶ℋ(𝜶(t))−∇𝜶ℋλ(𝜶(t),𝒘λ∗(𝜶(t))∥\displaystyle\leq D_{\mathcal{A}}\cdot\|\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\mathcal{H}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{(t)})-\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\mathcal{H}_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{(t)},\text{\boldmath{$w$}}_{\lambda}^{*}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}^{(t)})\|

Appendix B Derivation of the Hyper-gradient

To maintain self-containment and rigorously justify the connection discussed in Section 2.3, we provide the derivation of the hyper-gradient for our specific data selection formulation using the standard Implicit Function Theorem.

The bilevel optimization problem for data weighting is defined as:

min𝜶∈𝒜⁡ℒval​(𝒘⁡(𝜶))\displaystyle\min_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}\in\mathcal{A}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{val}}(\text{\boldmath{$w$}}(\boldsymbol{\alpha})) :=ℒval​(𝒘​(𝜶))\displaystyle:=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{val}}\left(\text{\boldmath{$w$}}(\boldsymbol{\alpha})\right)
s.t. 𝒘​(𝜶)∈arg⁡min𝒘​ℒtrain​(𝜶,𝒘)\displaystyle\text{ s.t. }\text{\boldmath{$w$}}(\boldsymbol{\alpha})\in\arg\min_{\boldsymbol{w}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{train}}(\boldsymbol{\alpha},\text{\boldmath{$w$}}) :=1γ​N​∑n=1N𝜶n​ℒtrainn​(𝒘).\displaystyle:=\frac{1}{\gamma N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{n}\mathcal{L}_{\text{train}}^{n}(\boldsymbol{w}).

To optimize this problem, we compute the hyper-gradient using the chain rule:

∇𝜶ℒval​(𝒘⁡(𝜶))=(∂𝒘⁡(𝜶)∂𝜶)T​∇𝒘ℒval​(𝒘)\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{val}}(\boldsymbol{w}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}))=\left(\frac{\partial\boldsymbol{w}(\boldsymbol{\alpha})}{\partial\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\right)^{T}\nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{val}}(\boldsymbol{w}) (28)

Assuming the inner optimization reaches a local minimum, the first-order optimality condition holds:

∇𝒘ℒtrain​(𝜶,𝒘⁡(𝜶))=𝟎\nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{train}}(\boldsymbol{\alpha},\boldsymbol{w}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}))=\mathbf{0}

Taking the total derivative with respect to 𝜶\boldsymbol{\alpha}, we get

∇𝜶​𝒘2​ℒtrain​(𝜶,𝒘)+∇𝒘​𝒘2​ℒtrain​(𝜶,𝒘)​∂𝒘⁡(𝜶)∂𝜶=𝟎\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}\boldsymbol{w}}^{2}\mathcal{L}_{\text{train}}(\boldsymbol{\alpha},\boldsymbol{w})+\nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}\boldsymbol{w}}^{2}\mathcal{L}_{\text{train}}(\boldsymbol{\alpha},\boldsymbol{w})\frac{\partial\boldsymbol{w}(\boldsymbol{\alpha})}{\partial\boldsymbol{\alpha}}=\mathbf{0}

Letting 𝑯=∇𝒘​𝒘2​ℒtrain​(𝜶,𝒘)\boldsymbol{H}=\nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}\boldsymbol{w}}^{2}\mathcal{L}_{\text{train}}(\boldsymbol{\alpha},\boldsymbol{w}) denote the Hessian matrix, we get the Jacobian:

∂𝒘⁡(𝜶)∂𝜶=−𝑯−1​∇𝜶​𝒘2ℒtrain​(𝜶,𝒘)\frac{\partial\boldsymbol{w}(\boldsymbol{\alpha})}{\partial\boldsymbol{\alpha}}=-\boldsymbol{H}^{-1}\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}\boldsymbol{w}}^{2}\mathcal{L}_{\text{train}}(\boldsymbol{\alpha},\boldsymbol{w}) (29)

Based on the inner objective, the gradient w.r.t. the model weights is:

∇𝒘ℒtrain​(𝜶,𝒘)=1γ​N​∑n=1N𝜶n​∇𝒘ℒtrainn​(𝒘)\nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{train}}(\boldsymbol{\alpha},\boldsymbol{w})=\frac{1}{\gamma N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{n}\nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{train}}^{n}(\boldsymbol{w})

Taking the derivative with respect to the hyper-parameters 𝜶\boldsymbol{\alpha}, we get:

∇𝜶​𝒘2​ℒtrain​(𝜶,𝒘∗)=1γ​N​𝑱train\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}\boldsymbol{w}}^{2}\mathcal{L}_{\text{train}}(\boldsymbol{\alpha},\boldsymbol{w}^{*})=\frac{1}{\gamma N}\boldsymbol{J}_{\text{train}}

where 𝑱train=[∇𝒘ℒtrain1​(𝒘),…,∇𝒘ℒtrainN​(𝒘)]\boldsymbol{J}_{\text{train}}=\left[\nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{train}}^{1}(\boldsymbol{w}),\dots,\nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{train}}^{N}(\boldsymbol{w})\right] is the matrix of individual training sample gradients. Substituting Equation (29) into Equation (28), we obtain the final hyper-gradient:

∇𝜶ℒval​(𝒘⁡(𝜶))=−1γ​N​𝑱trainT​𝑯−1​∇𝒘ℒval​(𝒘)\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{val}}(\boldsymbol{w}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}))=-\frac{1}{\gamma N}\boldsymbol{J}_{\text{train}}^{T}\boldsymbol{H}^{-1}\nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{val}}(\boldsymbol{w})

Thus for a certain entry, we have ∇𝜶nℒval​(𝒘⁡(𝜶))∝−∇𝒘ℒtrainn​(𝒘)T​𝑯−1​∇𝒘ℒval​(𝒘)\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\alpha}_{n}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{val}}(\boldsymbol{w}(\boldsymbol{\alpha}))\propto-\nabla_{\text{\boldmath{$w$}}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{train}}^{n}(\boldsymbol{w})^{T}\boldsymbol{H}^{-1}\nabla_{\boldsymbol{w}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{val}}(\boldsymbol{w}).

Appendix C Hyper-parameters

Hyper-parameter settings

The detailed hyper-parameters for the BLADE algorithms in the domain-shift continuous pre-training and general continious pre-training scenario are shown in Table 5.

While Theorem 1 and Lemma 1 establish that the penalized formulation strictly recovers the original bi-level objective as λ→∞\lambda\to\infty, employing an infinitely large penalty in practical deep learning inevitably leads to gradient explosion and numerical instability. In our BLADE framework, we mitigate this theory-practice gap through the periodic synchronization mechanism (𝒘0(e)=𝒖(e​τ)\text{\boldmath{$w$}}_{0}^{(e)}=\boldsymbol{u}^{(e\tau)}). Because the reference model 𝒘w and proxy model 𝒖\boldsymbol{u} are periodically realigned, their structural drift is bounded (as empirically verified in Figure 4(a)). This bounded disparity naturally constrains the penalty term. Consequently, we find that setting a smaller λ\lambda provides sufficient soft constraint to enforce the bi-level objective without destabilizing the optimization trajectory.

Appendix D Additional Experiments

D.1 The Transferability of the Selected Tokens

While BLADE effectively identifies high-quality training data, scoring and selecting data natively on massive LLMs introduces computational overhead. To further reduce the selection computation, we investigate whether data selected by a smaller proxy model is transferable. We train the 7B-parameter Llama2 model using the exact token pre-selected by BLADE on the 1.1B TinyLlama (denoted as BLADE-Tr). As shown in Table 6, BLADE-Tr achieves an average accuracy of 37.2, substantially outperforming the random sampling baseline (32.3) and naive continuous pre-train baseline (33.8). This indicates that data quality signals are partially model-agnostic and transferable. However, BLADE-Tr noticeably underperforms native BLADE on the 7B model (43.8). This gap demonstrates that optimal data selection is capacity-dependent. The 1.1B proxy model may misclassify "hard but learnable" samples as unlearnable noise, discarding data that would actually be highly informative for the 7B model. Therefore, while cross-scale data transfer is a viable low-cost compromise, fully unlocking a large model’s potential requires capacity-matched data selection and orchestration.
